OAS at 65 or later? Map the cash bridge before the larger monthly pension

Compare the OAS payments forgone from 65 with the permanent 0.6%-per-month increase for a later start. Four charts separate dated 2026 maximums, original cash-flow arithmetic, partial-pension assumptions and the GIS/Allowance eligibility gap.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare OAS start ages with a transparent gross cash bridge

Official anchor: Service Canada lists a maximum age-65 pension of CAD 762.50 per month for October–December 2026 and a 0.6% increase for each month after age 65, up to 36% at 70. The selected pension share is an editable teaching assumption, not an eligibility or residence calculation. Original arithmetic freezes today’s quarterly rate for every future payment and assumes 12 payments each year; actual OAS is adjusted quarterly for CPI. It excludes the separate 10% increase after age 75, tax/recovery tax, GIS, Allowance, other income, discounting, payment timing and mortality. The crossover is not a recommendation or forecast.

The central idea

Deferring OAS exchanges earlier cash for a higher monthly pension later. A simple crossover can help explain that exchange, but GIS eligibility, residence, tax, spending needs, inflation adjustments and longevity can change the household result.

01

Each month deferred raises the later monthly amount

Old Age Security (OAS) can start at age 65 or as late as age 70. Service Canada says the pension rises by 0.6% for each month after age 65: 7.2% for a full year and 36% after 60 months. This is a simple percentage increase against the age-65 pension—not monthly investment compounding.

For October to December 2026, Service Canada lists the maximum age-65-to-74 pension as CAD 762.50 per month. Applying the published deferral percentages gives CAD 817.40 at age 66 and CAD 1,037.00 at age 70. Those are dated maximums for a full pension before an individual income-related recovery tax; they are not guaranteed personal amounts. The payment is reviewed quarterly using the Consumer Price Index, so holding the 2026 dollar amount flat in a long-range chart is a teaching convention, not an estimate of future deposits.

OAS is separate from CPP. CPP may start earlier; OAS cannot start before 65. Delaying one benefit does not require delaying the other.

02

Count the bridge: payments skipped are real household cash flow

Suppose a person’s full age-65 OAS is CAD 762.50 each month and they delay to 70. Under a fixed-rate illustration, the 60 skipped months represent CAD 45,750 in gross OAS (60 × CAD 762.50), while the age-70 monthly amount is CAD 1,037.00. The monthly increase over the age-65 amount is CAD 274.50.

Dividing the CAD 45,750 bridge by CAD 274.50 gives 166⅔ months after the later pension starts—about 13 years and 11 months. In this simplified comparison, cumulative gross amounts catch up around age 83 years 11 months. The model below uses CAD 762.50, so its correctly recomputed 60-month foregone amount is CAD 45,750; a larger number would result only under a different base. This example is just the gross arithmetic and deliberately freezes the quarterly amount.

The editable chart shows cumulative cash by age instead of treating the crossover as a verdict. A household that uses the pension to pay essential expenses may value the early cash differently from a household with other reliable income. A longer lifespan can provide more months at the higher amount, but no one can know an individual lifespan in advance.

03

Check GIS and Allowance before comparing the OAS lines

Service Canada explicitly says there is no benefit to delaying OAS if you are eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS). While OAS is deferred, you cannot receive GIS, and your spouse or common-law partner cannot apply for the Allowance during that period. GIS and Allowance do not increase because OAS was deferred.

That eligibility gap can outweigh a simple OAS-only crossover. The article’s cash model intentionally does not invent a GIS amount or combine unrelated household benefits: GIS depends on marital status, income and the applicable payment period, and Allowance has its own age and household conditions. If either benefit may apply, compare the complete household cash-flow path using the official estimator or Service Canada rather than the OAS-only graph.

The 2026 table lists a maximum single-person GIS of CAD 1,138.90 monthly for October–December 2026 and a maximum OAS of CAD 762.50, but these ceilings have different income tests and eligibility conditions. They are not a promise that any one household can receive both maxima. The amounts also use different rules for determining income and should not be added casually.

04

Residence, age 75 and income can change the actual pension

OAS is based partly on residence in Canada after age 18. For someone living in Canada, Service Canada describes a partial-pension eligibility minimum of 10 years and a calculation based on years of residence divided by 40; someone living abroad generally needs 20 years, with international agreements potentially affecting eligibility. A person with 20 qualifying years could therefore receive a 50% share of the full pension under that basic fraction. Exact eligibility should be confirmed with the program.

Deferral increases the actual pension amount, but an increase applied to a partial entitlement does not turn it into a full pension. The interactive share control simply scales the published full amount to illustrate how proportional cash paths behave; it does not determine a claimant’s residence record, foreign coverage or entitlement.

At age 75, eligible OAS recipients receive a separate automatic 10% increase beginning the month after their birthday. It is distinct from the deferral increase, and Service Canada says it does not increase GIS. The cash illustration does not include this age-75 adjustment, so its lines are not a projection of future OAS deposits.

OAS is taxable, and the recovery tax may reduce or eliminate payment above the applicable net-world-income threshold. The October–December 2026 table uses 2025 income thresholds. The OAS recovery-tax guide explains the tax-year and payment-calendar relationship; estimates should use the thresholds and household facts for the relevant tax year.

05

Build a decision around the whole retirement plan

Before selecting a start age, compare current cash needs, other reliable income, health and longevity uncertainty, tax, and possible GIS or partner Allowance eligibility. Consider the funding source for the years when OAS will not arrive. Drawing registered assets to bridge a deferral may affect taxable income and future income-tested benefits; using cash or a TFSA can create a different tax path. These interactions deserve a year-by-year projection rather than a single crossover age.

Use the charts to inspect the mechanics: choose an OAS start age, adjust the assumed share of a full pension, and move the comparison horizon. The model treats payments as 12 full monthly deposits per year at a constant rate. It excludes CPI indexation, tax, recovery tax, GIS, Allowance, discounting, partial-month timing, survivor effects and mortality. The fixed-rate crossover is not a break-even recommendation and does not model uncertainty.

For an individual estimate, use Service Canada’s OAS Benefits Estimator and verify residence history, income and program eligibility directly. If you are eligible for GIS, or your partner may qualify for the Allowance, ask Service Canada to compare the consequences before choosing to delay.
